paragraphs.heading: Mud between the tides
paragraphs.text: A tidal flat, also called a mudflat, is a coastal wetland made of sediment that tides or rivers have dropped. It forms in the intertidal zone, and because most of its sediment sits there, the flat goes under the sea and comes back out roughly twice a day. In Ireland people call these places slob or slobs.

paragraphs.heading: Where they form
paragraphs.text: Tidal flats build up in sheltered spots such as bays, bayous, lagoons and estuaries. They also appear in freshwater lakes and in salty inland seas where rivers and creeks run out. Geologists can think of a flat as a layer of bay mud left exposed, made from estuary silt, clay and the remains of water animals. Rivers supply most of the silt.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of sand and mud
paragraphs.text: The deposits gather in the intertidal zone, which has two parts: a bare stretch and marshes. The bare stretch runs from the lowest part of the intertidal zone up to the marsh. Near the tidal bars its layers are mostly sand, and they grow muddier along the tidal channels. In the marshes, many herbaceous plants grow on thin layers of sand and mud, and their decaying remains are where coal and peat layers begin.

paragraphs.heading: How big and where
paragraphs.text: A 2019 global study suggested tidal flats cover at least 127,921 km² of Earth, about as much as mangroves. Roughly half of that area lies in just eight countries, among them Indonesia, China, Australia and the United States. Asia alone holds 44% of the world's tidal flats.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Together with salt marshes and mangrove forests, tidal flats are important ecosystems. They support plenty of wildlife and can be vital to some crabs, mollusks and fish. They are a key habitat that lets tens of millions of shorebirds travel between breeding sites in the northern hemisphere and non-breeding areas in the southern hemisphere. Keeping the flats intact also helps prevent coastal erosion.

paragraphs.heading: Shrinking ground
paragraphs.text: People once saw tidal flats as having little economic value and often dredged them to make farmland. Today they are threatened by rising seas, land claimed for development, dredging for shipping and chemical pollution. Around the Yellow Sea in East Asia, over 65% of the mudflats that existed in the early 1950s were gone by the late 2000s. Worldwide, as much as 16% of tidal flats may have vanished since the mid-1980s.

paragraphs.heading: A trap underfoot
paragraphs.text: Some mudflats are very dangerous to cross. Near Anchorage, Alaska, the flats are made of fine glacial silt that holds on to its water. The ground looks firm, but a footstep can turn it to something like quicksand. Four people are known to have been caught there up to the waist and drowned as the tide rose.
